overview.title: 📖 Overview: Protest, Retribution, and Reinterpreting Scripture
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 55a–55b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין מִיתָה בְּלֹא חֵטְא, וְאֵין יִסּוּרִין בְּלֹא עָוֹן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Continuing the theme that one who could protest wrongdoing and did not is held responsible, the Gemara tells of Rabbi Zeira urging Rabbi Simon to rebuke the Exilarch's household even if they will not listen, and cites the dramatic vision of Ezekiel 9, where God marks the righteous for protection and the wicked for destruction — then retracts that protection once He is reminded the righteous, too, failed to protest. This launches a survey of when the Patriarchs' merit ceased to protect Israel, then a debate over whether death and suffering always signal personal sin, tested against Moses, Aaron, and four others said to have died only because of Adam's sin. The daf closes with the sages defending the reputations of biblical figures, beginning with Reuben.

slides.title: 📜 Marking the Righteous and the Wicked
slides.subtitle: Ezekiel's vision, and the one good decree God ever retracted

nodes.content: 🕊️ God tells Gabriel: mark the righteous with an ink Tav (protection), the wicked with a blood Tav (for destroying angels)
❓ Midat HaDin (Divine Justice) asks: what is the difference between these and those?
🗣️ God: these are fully righteous, those fully wicked. Midat HaDin: but the righteous could have protested the wicked's sins, and did not!

columns.label: God's defense
columns.content: I know their protest would not have been accepted

columns.label: Midat HaDin's reply
columns.content: It was known to You — but was it known to them?

nodes.content: 💔 God retracts: even the righteous who failed to protest are struck, starting from those closest to the Sanctuary — the fully devoted

callout.label: Rabbi Aḥa bar Ḥanina:
callout.text: Never did a good decree leave God's mouth and get reversed for the worse — except this one.

slides.title: ⏳ When Did the Patriarchs' Merit Cease?
slides.subtitle: Four sages locate the turning point at four different biblical moments
rows: 'I will uncover her lewdness... none shall deliver her from My hand' (Hosea 2:12)
God was gracious to Israel 'because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob' (II Kings 13:23) — the last such mention
'Let it be known this day' — implying not afterward (I Kings 18:36)
'From now and forever the zeal of the Lord... performs this' (Isaiah 9:6) — zeal replaces ancestral merit

callout.label: Shared premise:
callout.text: All four agree the merit did eventually run out; they disagree only about the historical marker.

slides.title: ⚖️ Is There Death Without Sin?
slides.subtitle: Rav Ami's principle meets a sharp challenge

lines.speaker: Rav Ami
lines.text: There is no death without sin, and no suffering without iniquity — proven from Ezekiel 18:20 and Psalms 89:33.

lines.speaker: Angels
lines.text: Then why did Moses and Aaron, who observed the entire Torah, still die? God answered only: 'One event befalls the righteous and the wicked' (Ecclesiastes 9:2) — implying death is not always tied to sin!

lines.speaker: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
lines.text: Even Moses and Aaron died for their own sin — 'Because you did not believe in Me' (Numbers 20:12). Had they believed, their time would not yet have come.

lines.speaker: Gemara's conclusion
lines.text: The baraita listing four who died sinless can only follow Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar — meaning death without sin does exist elsewhere. This is a conclusive refutation of Rav Ami.

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Rav Ami's sweeping principle is rejected — some people do die, or suffer, without any sin of their own.

slides.title: 🐍 Four Who Died Only Because of the Serpent
slides.subtitle: Righteous individuals whose deaths trace to Adam's sin, not their own

steps.content: 4️⃣ Kilab, son of David — Yishai's case alone has an explicit proof: Abigail is called 'daughter of Nahash (serpent)' though she was really Yishai's daughter, teaching Yishai died only for the serpent's sin

callout.label: Significance:
callout.text: This baraita, like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view, assumes death can occur without the deceased's own sin — the very point that refutes Rav Ami.

slides.title: 🤔 Did Reuben Sin With Bilhah?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani's exoneration, and the tannaitic dispute it rests on

boxes.title: Innocent
items: 'The sons of Jacob were twelve' — all equally righteous even after the incident
He merely rearranged his father's bed, protesting the honor of his mother Leah
Aḥerim: he rearranged two beds — his father's and the Divine Presence's
Pachaz read backwards: 'you trembled, you recoiled, sin fled from you'

boxes.title: Guilty
items: Rabbi Eliezer: Pachaz = 'you were impulsive, liable, contemptuous'
Rabbi Yehoshua: Pachaz = 'you trampled the law, sinned, were promiscuous'
The plain sense of 'he lay with Bilhah his father's concubine' supports this reading

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: Rabban Gamliel objects: could Reuben's own tribe stand at Mount Eival and curse 'cursed is he who lies with his father's wife' if their ancestor had truly done so?

summary.principle: Failing to protest wrongdoing one could have stopped brings shared responsibility — even for the righteous — and the sages read biblical narratives, including claims of death without sin, in light of that same demand for moral accountability.

flowSteps.content: 📜 God marks the righteous for protection — until reminded they too failed to protest the wicked
⏳ The Patriarchs' protective merit eventually ran out, per four different sages' timelines

columns.content: ⚖️ Rav Ami's 'no death without sin' is refuted by the deaths of Moses, Aaron, and four sinless others
🤔 Reuben's reputation is defended by one tannaitic view, questioned by another

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: whoever can protest wrongdoing and fails to becomes implicated in it, even the otherwise righteous

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Aḥa bar Ḥanina, what is unique about God's decree in Ezekiel 9 to mark the righteous for protection?
o: It is the only decree ever given through an angel
It is the only good decree God ever retracted and turned to something bad
It only applied to the tribe of Levi
It was the first decree given after the Exodus
quiz.e: Rabbi Aḥa bar Ḥanina states that this is the only time a promise of good that emerged from God was later retracted and rendered evil, once Midat HaDin pointed out that the righteous too had failed to protest.

quiz.q: Why does Midat HaDin argue that the righteous should not be fully protected in Ezekiel's vision?
o: They committed the same sins as the wicked
They had the ability to protest the wicked's conduct and did not do so
They were not actually righteous
They failed to bring sacrifices
quiz.e: Midat HaDin points out that it was in the power of the righteous to protest the sinful conduct around them, yet they did not, making them partially responsible.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara ultimately refute Rav Ami's claim that there is no death or suffering without sin?
o: By citing a verse that explicitly contradicts him
By showing that a baraita listing four people who died only because of Adam's sin (not their own) follows a view compatible with death occurring without personal sin
By proving Rav Ami never made this statement
By citing a dissenting opinion of Rav Ami himself
quiz.e: The baraita about four people who died solely due to Adam's sin with the serpent, while personally sinless, directly contradicts Rav Ami's principle, leading the Gemara to declare it a conclusive refutation (teyuvta).

quiz.q: What textual proof does the Gemara bring that Yishai, father of David, died only because of the serpent's sin?
o: A direct verse stating so explicitly
Abigail is called 'daughter of Nahash (the serpent)' even though she was actually Yishai's daughter
The Talmud simply states it as an oral tradition with no proof
A comparison to Moses' death
quiz.e: Since Abigail was demonstrably the daughter of Yishai (per Chronicles), her being called 'daughter of Nahash' is understood homiletically to mean she was the daughter of one who died because of the serpent's sin, i.e., Yishai.

quiz.q: According to Rabban Gamliel's argument in defense of Reuben, why is it implausible that Reuben actually sinned with Bilhah?
o: Because the Torah never mentions Bilhah
Because Reuben's own descendants, the tribe of Reuben, would later stand at Mount Eival and curse anyone who lies with his father's wife
Because Bilhah died before the incident could occur
Because Jacob forbade any discussion of the matter
quiz.e: Rabban Gamliel reasons that it is inconceivable Reuben's own tribe would later curse 'he who lies with his father's wife' at Mount Eival if their ancestor had actually committed that sin.
